query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Although many physical and chemical fabrication methods have been developed, synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly understood, limiting assessment of these materials for high-temperature applications. The hypothesis should remain compatible with a multielement solid solution and the potential for catalytic performance at low noble-metal content. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to untreated nanoparticles, the application and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment with a clear failure criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a refractory element, such as tungsten, into the composition of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles can enhance their stability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals
generation.intervention: Addition of a refractory element, such as tungsten, to the nanoparticle composition
generation.conditions: Operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a single-phase solid solution with refined grain structure
generation.mechanism: The refractory element enhances the stability of the nanoparticles by reducing grain growth and increasing the lattice distortion, which in turn improves the catalytic performance and durability
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved stability and catalytic performance of the nanoparticles during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime
generation.baseline: Untreated nanoparticles with no refractory element addition
generation.boundary: Compositional boundary: near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals; Application boundary: catalytic regime of 773–1173 K
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the refractory element's effect on the nanoparticle stability and catalytic performance is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the stability and catalytic performance of nanoparticles with and without the addition of a refractory element, such as tungsten, in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of a refractory element does not improve the stability and catalytic performance of the nanoparticles, the hypothesis is falsified

Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles be synthesized at low temperatures on conventional supports, and what mechanisms govern their formation and catalytic performance in CO2 hydrogenation?. System: CoNiCuRuPd high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on TiO2 (CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2); comparison with CoNiCuRuPd/Al2O3, CoNiCuRuPd/MgO, and monometallic Pd/TiO2, Ru/TiO2, Co/TiO2, Ni/TiO2, Cu/TiO2. Processing: Simple impregnation of TiO2 with aqueous solutions of Co(NO3)2·6H2O, Ni(NO3)2·6H2O, Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, RuCl3·nH2O, and Na2PdCl4 (1:1:1:1:1 molar ratio; Pd 1.0 wt%); reduction under H2 flow (20 mL/min) at 400 °C for 2 h without prior calcination. Test conditions: CO2 hydrogenation at atmospheric pressure, 300–400 °C, with N2/H2/CO2 mixture (4/5/1 composition, total flow 50 mL/min, SV = 6000 mL/g/h); stability tested over 72 h; in situ XAFS and XRD under H2 at 200–400 °C; H2-TPR from 50 to 600 °C at 5 °C/min; CO-TPD and FTIR; TEM/STEM/EDX; ETEM under 300 kV electron beam; DFT and MD simulations at 900 K.
